title: The heart among dharma's roots
word: with the Keeper's framing of what
hook: Yudhishthira at the yaksha's lake: what is the path? and a law book that names the heart among dharma's roots
carry: the heart is a root of dharma
tomorrow: so is weighing it all just picking and choosing?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambedkar's fire: untouchability is abolished, and a book refused in public. Now, a question asked at a lake.

Yudhishthira's four brothers lie still beside a lake. Each one drank before answering the voice that guards it. Now the voice, a yaksha, puts its questions to him, and his brothers' lives hang on the answers. One of them: what is the path? He answers, in paraphrase: reasoning doesn't settle it; the scriptures differ; no single sage's word is final; the truth of dharma is hidden in a cave. The path is the one the great have walked. The yaksha is pleased, and in the end gives all four brothers back.
screen: `FOUR BROTHERS BY A LAKE.` → `WHAT IS THE PATH?` → `THE WAY THE GREAT HAVE WALKED.`

segments.voice: The Manusmriti says something close, and then goes one step further. Its second chapter opens by calling dharma what good people, free of hatred and grasping, approve in their hearts. Then it names the roots of dharma. In paraphrase: the Veda, the smriti, the conduct of good people, and what is pleasing to one's own self. Four roots, and the last is the surprise. Commentators call it atmatushti, the self's contentment. Readers take it in different ways. Some read it narrowly: it counts only where the first three leave a choice open. Others hear in it a place for conscience inside the tradition. A neighbor tradition says something close. In his letter to the Romans, Paul writes of people who don't have the law yet do what it asks, and who, in the King James words, "shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness." An honest difference: Paul speaks of people outside the law; Manu puts the heart inside a law book, last of four roots. Both leave room for the heart. So when a rule and your gut pull apart, the Hindu answer isn't 'just follow your gut'. It's the Veda, the remembered books, the way the good have walked, and then a heart shaped by them.
screen: `MANU: WHAT THE GOOD APPROVE.` · `FOUR ROOTS: VEDA, SMRITI, THE GOOD, THE HEART.` · `ROMANS: WRITTEN IN THEIR HEARTS.` · then, large: `THE HEART IS A ROOT OF DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, and bring to mind one choice in front of you right now. Without deciding anything, notice what sits easy in your heart and what doesn't, the way you'd notice warm air and cool. If you pray, you can hold the choice before God.
Kept and rejected, weighed by a root inside the law: atmatushti, the self's contentment, last of Manu's four roots of dharma.
Your line: the heart is a root of dharma, atmatushti, last of four, after the Veda, the remembered books and the way of the good. More tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers sometimes point to Manu's list of the roots of dharma, the Veda, tradition, good conduct and the self's contentment, when talking about conscience in Hindu ethics; some Christians turn to Romans 2:14–15 when they speak of conscience.

Unity thread (wisdom day, and this month's meeting with the best friend's family): shared with Christianity, in its own words (Romans 2:15, KJV): right and wrong written within a person. Honest difference: Paul speaks of Gentiles without the law whose conscience bears witness (2:14); Manu places the self's contentment inside a law book, last of four roots. Neither ranked; not 'all the same'. 1574 used Judaism (Leviticus 19), so this week's neighbor differs. Sam's grandmother (Christian family, per earlier notes) quotes the line in the chat.

KJV Romans 2:15 reads 'Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another;' the quotation uses the middle of the verse exactly. Confirm.
'Four roots' is the text's own count (2.12 calls them fourfold). Manu's wording is 'ātmanas tuṣṭi' (2.6) and 'svasya ca priyam ātmanaḥ' (2.12); 'atmatushti' is the commentators' term. Confirm.
'Some read it narrowly… others hear a place for conscience' summarizes a known range of readings (e.g. commentators who limit it to optional matters); confirm or name.
